primary_claim: SAE probes do not consistently beat activation-probe baselines on held-out test AUC and are not a useful addition to a practitioner's toolkit, though the earlier version of this work had found SAE probes competitive with and sometimes advantageous over baselines in low-data, corrupted-label, and interpretability settings

effect.metric: % of dataset/training-size comparisons where SAE probe beats baseline (test ROC AUC)
effect.value: 27% overall, rising to 35% in data-scarce settings (<34 training examples)

contradicts_or_qualifies: Anthropic's finding (features-as-classifiers update) that SAE probes can outperform activation probes on OOD data, though the authors note that work reports no margins of error and uses only a single dataset
stated_future_work: test with 1024 training examples instead of confounding data efficiency with class imbalance
test the setting with imbalanced training classes but balanced test classes
apply SAE probes to real-world label-noise case studies such as probing for truthfulness
use larger SAEs as they become publicly available
limitations_stated: all experiments run on a single layer (20) of Gemma 2 9B base
did not do extensive optimization in the label-noise setting (e.g. softening class encodings)
OOD findings are preliminary, based on only 8 datasets
no strong hypothesis for why imbalanced-class SAE probes don't outperform baselines
quote: We find that SAE probes do not consistently beat baselines on test AUC and are not a useful addition to a practitioner's toolkit.
